subtype: Approach: report to the company and cybercrime portal when misuse appears [Revision]
passage:
I'm Binita, and I share a flat with Mridul. Last Tuesday he was scrolling his bank messages at breakfast and went quiet. There was a payment on his account he didn't recognise. He didn't shout or say much. He just took screenshots of the message and the statement, then phoned the bank and asked for the card to be blocked.

That evening I watched him fill in the cybercrime portal form and write down the reference number on a sticky note. Then he wrote to the shop whose breach had leaked his details, attaching the same screenshots.

I can't tell how scared he felt. He looked pale but steady. All I know is that by bedtime the whole thing was on file in three places.

qa.q: Where did Mridul write down the reference number?
How might Mridul have felt when he saw the unfamiliar payment, and how sure is Binita?
qa.a: Mridul probably felt shocked and worried, though Binita admits it cannot be known for sure, as he looked pale but steady.

qa.q: What could Mridul do next to keep the case moving, and why?
qa.a: Mridul could keep the reference number and screenshots safe and follow up with the bank and the shop, because each report can be checked against the same evidence.

qa.q: How does Binita see Mridul's response compared with panicking?
qa.a: Binita saw a calm, methodical flatmate who moved from prevention to reporting, and probably felt reassured watching it.

grounding: When a suspicious transaction appears, the person moves from prevention to reporting to the bank, the cybercrime portal and the leaking service.

passage:
Day 1, Monday. A notice from the gaming site Harish plays on says card details may have leaked. He changes his password, turns on two-step login, and decides that's enough.
Day 9, Tuesday. At 7:10 a.m. a text from his bank: ₹4,200 spent at an online electronics shop he has never used. His stomach drops. He calls his friend Sahil, who says, 'This is different now. Stop preventing. Start reporting.' Harish screenshots the text, the bank app entry and the breach notice. He calls the number on the back of his card; the bank blocks it and raises a dispute. At 8:15 he files a complaint on the national cybercrime portal and notes the number. At 9:00 he emails the gaming site's support, attaching everything.
Day 12, Friday. The bank emails: the ₹4,200 has been temporarily credited back while they investigate. The gaming site replies with an apology and a case ID. Harish saves everything in one folder.

qa.q: How much was spent at the online electronics shop?
qa.a: ₹4,200 spent at an online electronics shop.

qa.q: How did Harish feel when the bank text arrived?
qa.a: His stomach dropped; he was alarmed that the leak had turned into real misuse.

qa.q: Why did Harish take screenshots before reporting?
qa.a: They gave the bank, the cybercrime portal and the gaming site the same clear evidence, making each complaint easier to act on.

qa.q: How does Sahil's advice change what Harish does?
qa.a: Sahil tells him prevention is no longer enough, which pushes Harish to report to all three places that morning.

grounding: Shows a young person moving from prevention to reporting when a suspicious transaction appears, complaining to the bank, the cybercrime portal and the leaking site with screenshots.

passage:
Imran, you keep saying the breach email was months ago and nothing has happened, so you're fine. Let your Sarita aunty tell you how I learned it isn't over till it's over.
When I was twenty-two, a travel site I'd used leaked data. I changed my password and forgot about it. Four months later, on a Sunday, I saw a ₹6,000 hotel booking on my card statement, in a city I'd never visited.
My hands went cold. Then I did what my father had drilled into me: take pictures first. I screenshotted the statement and the old breach email. I called the bank on the number on my card, and they blocked it. That afternoon I went to the cyber cell at the police station with printouts, and I emailed the travel site too, with everything attached.
The bank officer told me later that because I reported everything the same day, with proof, the money came back in three weeks.
So keep that breach email, Imran. And if anything strange appears, report it everywhere, that same day.

qa.q: How much was the hotel booking?
How did young Sarita feel on seeing the booking?
qa.a: Sarita's hands went cold with shock and fear, before a steadier resolve to act took over.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped get the money back?
qa.a: Reporting to the bank, the cyber cell and the travel site the same day, with screenshots, as the bank officer later confirmed.

qa.q: How might the bank officer have seen young Sarita's report?
qa.a: As a clear, well-documented case, which made it easier to investigate and refund quickly.

grounding: Shows a young person switching from prevention to reporting when misuse appears, with screenshots to the bank, the police cyber cell and the leaking site.
